{{short description|There are arbitrarily large computable gaps in the hierarchy of complexity classes}}
:''See also [[Gap theorem (disambiguation)]] for other gap theorems in [[mathematics]].''

In [[computational complexity theory]], the '''gap theorem,''' also known as the '''Borodin–Trakhtenbrot gap theorem,''' is a major theorem about the complexity of [[computable function]]s.<ref>{{Cite journal
 |first1        = Lance
 |last1         = Fortnow
|author1link = Lance Fortnow
 |first2       = Steve
 |last2        = Homer
 |title        = A Short History of Computational Complexity
 |url          = http://theorie.informatik.uni-ulm.de/Personen/toran/beatcs/column80.pdf
 |archive-url  = https://web.archive.org/web/20051229063702/http://theorie.informatik.uni-ulm.de/Personen/toran/beatcs/column80.pdf
 |url-status     = dead
 |archive-date = 2005-12-29
 |journal      = [[Bulletin of the European Association for Theoretical Computer Science]]
 |pages        = 95–133
 |issue        = 80
 |date         = June 2003
}}</ref>

It essentially states that there are arbitrarily large computable gaps in the hierarchy of [[complexity class]]es.  For any [[computable function]] that represents an increase in [[computational resource]]s, one can find a resource bound such that the set of functions computable within the expanded resource bound is the same as the set computable within the original bound.

The theorem was proved independently by [[Boris Trakhtenbrot]]<ref>{{cite book|last=Trakhtenbrot|first=Boris A.|title=The Complexity of Algorithms and Computations (Lecture Notes)|date=1967|publisher=Novosibirsk University}}</ref> and [[Allan Borodin]].<ref>{{cite book | last = Borodin | first = Allan | author-link = Allan Borodin | editor1-last = Fischer | editor1-first = Patrick C. | editor2-last = Ginsburg | editor2-first = Seymour | editor3-last = Harrison | editor3-first = Michael A. | contribution = Complexity classes of recursive functions and the existence of complexity gaps | pages = 67–78 | publisher = Association for Computing Machinery | title = Proceedings of the 1st Annual [[ACM Symposium on Theory of Computing]], May 5–7, 1969, Marina del Rey, CA, USA | year = 1969}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author=Borodin, Allan|title=Computational complexity and the existence of complexity gaps|journal=[[Journal of the ACM]]|volume=19|issue=1|pages=158–174|date=January 1972 |doi=10.1145/321679.321691|doi-access=free|hdl=1813/5899|hdl-access=free}}</ref>
Although Trakhtenbrot's derivation preceded Borodin's by several years, it was not known nor recognized in [[Western world#Cold War context|the West]] until after Borodin's work was published.

== Statement ==
As an introductory example, suppose that we are considering [[time complexity]] of a certain specific [[Turing machine]] model. The set <math>\operatorname{TIME}(n^2)</math> is the set of total computable functions, such that there exists some implementation of the function that computes it in time <math>\le n^2</math> given an input size of <math>n</math>. 

In general, any total computable function <math>t</math> defines some <math>\operatorname{TIME}(t(n))</math> time complexity class, and we expect that if <math>t'(n)</math> is much larger than <math>t(n)</math>, for all <math>n</math>, then <math>\operatorname{TIME}(t'(n))</math> should be larger than <math>\operatorname{TIME}(t(n))</math>. The gap theorem states that this is not necessarily so. Indeed, for any total computable <math>g</math> such that <math>g(n) > n</math> for all <math>n</math>, there exists some total computable function <math>t</math>, such that <math>\operatorname{TIME}(t(n)) = \operatorname{TIME}(g(t(n)))</math>. Intuitively, adding compute time might not allow us to compute more functions.

More generally, suppose {{math|&Phi;}} is an [[Blum axioms|abstract (Blum) complexity measure]], then for any [[total computable function]] {{mvar|g}} for which <math>g(x) \geq x</math> for every {{mvar|x}}, there is a total computable function {{mvar|t}} such that with respect to {{math|&Phi;}}, the [[complexity class]]es with boundary functions {{mvar|t}} and <math>g \circ t</math> are identical.

=== Implications ===
For the special case of time complexity, this can be stated more simply as:
:for any total computable function <math>g : \, \omega \,\to\, \omega</math> such that <math>g(x) \geq x</math> for all {{mvar|x}}, there exists a time bound <math>T(n)</math> such that <math>\mathsf{DTIME}(g(T(n))) = \mathsf{DTIME}(T(n))</math>.
Similarly for the special case of [[space complexity]].

Because the bound {{tmath|T(n)}} may be very large (and often will be [[constructible function|nonconstructible]]) the gap theorem does not imply anything interesting for complexity classes such as [[P (complexity)|P]] or [[NP (complexity)|NP]],<ref>{{cite book|title=Computing Handbook, Third Edition: Computer Science and Software Engineering|editor1-first=Teofilo|editor1-last=Gonzalez|editor1-link= Teofilo F. Gonzalez |editor2-first=Jorge|editor2-last=Diaz-Herrera|editor3-first=Allen|editor3-last=Tucker|publisher=CRC Press|year=2014|isbn=9781439898529|contribution=Chapter 7: Complexity Theory|first1=Eric W.|last1=Allender|authorlink1=Eric Allender|first2=Michael C.|last2=Loui|first3=Kenneth W.|last3=Regan|page=7{{hyphen}}9|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=vMqSAwAAQBAJ&pg=SA7-PA9|quote=Fortunately, the gap phenomenon cannot happen for time bounds ''t'' that anyone would ever be interested in}}.</ref> and it does not contradict the [[time hierarchy theorem]] or [[space hierarchy theorem]].<ref>{{cite book|title=Computational Complexity: A Quantitative Perspective|volume=196|series=North-Holland Mathematics Studies|first=Marius|last=Zimand|publisher=Elsevier|year=2004|isbn=9780080476667|page=42|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=j-nhMYoZhgYC&pg=PA42}}.</ref>
